name: Media
blurb: Generation tools transformed production while training-data litigation transformed the business relationship with AI; cross-linked to the lawsuit tracker.

points.desc: The US Copyright Office AI policy programme, covering registrability of AI-assisted works, training on copyrighted material, and digital replicas, is the primary legal reference for anyone publishing AI-assisted media in the United States.
points.name: The Copyright Office is writing the rules

points.desc: Article 50 of the EU AI Act sets transparency obligations for AI-generated and manipulated content, including deepfakes. It applies to publishers distributing into the EU regardless of where the content was made.
points.name: Synthetic media carries a disclosure duty in the EU

points.desc: C2PA publishes the open technical specification for content credentials: cryptographically signed provenance that travels with an image, video, or audio file. It is the standards-body answer to the question of what a newsroom attaches to a synthetic asset.
points.name: Provenance is being standardised, not invented per outlet

points.desc: The Associated Press documents its own AI use in production, including transcription, shotlisting, and metadata. It is an operating newsroom describing deployed systems rather than a vendor describing a roadmap.
points.name: A wire service publishing what it actually does

points.desc: AP publishes its standards for generative AI in journalism, covering what may be produced with it, what must be verified, and what may not be published. One of the few newsroom policies available to read in full rather than summarised.
points.name: Newsroom rules written down and published

points.desc: The Reuters Institute Digital News Report at Oxford surveys news consumption across dozens of markets, including audience trust in AI-assisted journalism and newsroom adoption. Survey-based and published in full.
points.name: Audience data on AI in news, measured annually

points.desc: The Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia publishes research on algorithmic distribution, newsroom tools, and the business ethics of AI in media, independent of the vendors selling the tools.
points.name: Independent research on newsroom AI tooling

points.desc: The Stanford HAI AI Index tracks technical progress, investment, and adoption annually, with data points covering creative media and journalism. Useful for placing a media-specific claim against the wider trend.
points.name: The field-wide numbers, including creative work

summary: Generation tools transformed production while training-data litigation transformed the business relationship with AI.

analysis.body:
According to the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 46.0% of firms in the Information sector reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 45.0% the prior period, making this one of the higher-adoption segments of the economy by that measure. The figure covers the broad NAICS 51 classification, which includes publishing, broadcasting, and related activities, so the number reflects a wide range of firm types and sizes rather than newsrooms alone.

Within journalism specifically, the Associated Press documents a range of deployed systems rather than aspirational plans. AP uses AI-driven tools to analyze video content and generate shotlists, operates a system called Merlin that recognizes elements within photos and videos without relying on descriptions or metadata, and collaborates with AppliedXL to analyze federal registry data and surface actionable news tips for local newsrooms. The AP is also working with ShortTok on AI-powered content discovery and video curation. Across all of these uses, AP states that any output from a generative AI tool must be treated as unvetted source material, that editorial judgment must be applied before publication, and that generative AI may not be used to add or subtract elements from photos, video, or audio.

On the standards and governance side, the regulatory picture is developing simultaneously in two jurisdictions. The U.S. Copyright Office has been conducting a multi-part study since 2023 covering the registrability of AI-assisted works, the use of copyrighted material in training, and digital replicas, with Part 1 published July 31, 2024, Part 2 on January 29, 2025, and a pre-publication version of Part 3 released May 9, 2025. That study, per the Copyright Office, is the primary legal reference for anyone publishing AI-assisted content in the United States. In the European Union, Article 50 of the EU AI Act imposes transparency obligations on providers and deployers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video, or text, requiring that outputs be marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated, and requiring disclosure when deepfake content is deployed. These obligations apply to publishers distributing into the EU regardless of where the content originates.

A technical answer to provenance questions is being advanced by the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity, known as C2PA, which publishes an open standard called Content Credentials. The specification provides cryptographically signed provenance metadata that travels with a digital file, functioning, in C2PA's own description, like a nutrition label for digital content. This is a standards-body solution rather than a proprietary one, meaning a newsroom adopting it is implementing a shared infrastructure rather than a single vendor's system.

Litigation is a live constraint on the sector. The AI lawsuit tracker maintained by theworldofai.org follows 103 active cases, with recent activity involving Perplexity AI, Runway AI, Stability AI, and X.AI, among others, across copyright and other claims. The Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia publishes independent research on algorithmic distribution and the business ethics of AI in media, and the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism at Oxford surveys audience attitudes toward AI-assisted journalism annually through its Digital News Report. A decision-maker evaluating AI deployment in a media context should weigh the regulatory compliance requirements in both the U.S. and EU, the unresolved training-data copyright questions, the operational governance that AP's published standards illustrate, and the provenance infrastructure that C2PA provides, before treating the Census adoption figure as a signal that deployment is straightforwardly routine.
